dishes.method: Cut the guanciale into strips or cubes and render it slowly until crisp. Beat the yolks with grated Pecorino Romano and black pepper. Toss the drained pasta with the guanciale and its fat, then take the pan off the heat and stir in the egg and cheese mixture with a little starchy pasta water until it forms a glossy cream that does not scramble. The creaminess comes only from egg, cheese, fat and starch.
dishes.game_blurb: Rome's most argued-over pasta: guanciale, egg yolk, Pecorino Romano and black pepper. Its silky sauce comes from technique, not cream.
dishes.game_method: Render guanciale until crisp. Whisk yolks with grated Pecorino and plenty of black pepper. Toss hot spaghetti with the guanciale and its fat, then, off the heat, stir in the egg mix with a splash of pasta water until glossy, not scrambled.

intruders.why: In carbonara the creaminess comes from egg yolks, Pecorino, guanciale fat and starchy pasta water. Italian chefs say added cream makes the dish greasier and flattens its flavor. It is the most common complaint about carbonara made outside Italy.
intruders.game_line: Carbonara gets its cream from egg yolk, Pecorino and pasta water — never from a carton.
intruders.contested_note: Nobody seriously defends it today, but cream appeared in Italian cookbook carbonaras in past decades: Unione Sarda reports that Gualtiero Marchesi's 1989 recipe used a quarter litre of cream for 400 g of spaghetti (editor search snippet). Dissapore reportedly cites older cookbooks (Carnacina, Guarnaschelli Gotti) with cream (influencer sweep). It is a habit Italy has abandoned, not a living regional variant.

dishes.method: Toast cracked black pepper in a pan and loosen it with some starchy pasta water. Separately, mix finely grated Pecorino Romano with a little warm (not boiling) pasta water into a smooth cream, because too much heat makes it clump. Finish the pasta in the pepper water, then off the heat toss in the Pecorino cream, adding cooking water until it coats the pasta. These three ingredients plus the water are the whole dish.
dishes.game_blurb: Three ingredients and nowhere to hide: Pecorino Romano, black pepper and starchy pasta water whipped into a cream. A Roman shepherds' dish.

intruders.why: Italians widely follow an unwritten rule: no grated aged cheese such as Parmigiano or Pecorino on fish and shellfish pasta, because it covers the delicate taste of the clams. In a 2022 YouGov survey, Italians gave cheese on seafood pasta a net score of -39. Asking for cheese on spaghetti alle vongole is the classic tourist mistake in Italian restaurants.
intruders.game_line: No cheese on clams: in a YouGov poll Italians rated cheese on seafood pasta -39.
intruders.contested_note: This is a custom, not a law. According to Scatti di Gusto and Gambero Rosso, Pellegrino Artusi's 19th-century recipe for spaghetti with telline (small clams) used butter and Parmigiano, but Artusi wrote from Florence, not Naples. Il Fatto Alimentare argues that Italy has no traditional ban on fish with cheese, only local habits, citing dishes such as Piedmont's razza al formaggio; the Parmigiano Reggiano consortium listed fish dishes where cheese works (2019). Even Vincenzo's Plate calls it a strong pattern rather than a strict law. For Neapolitan spaghetti alle vongole, though, the no-cheese rule is close to universal.

verification_limits: No source page was opened by any agent. Page fetching was blocked in this environment (DNS/policy failures on every host tried, including gamberorosso.it, dissapore.com, eur-lex.europa.eu, pizzanapoletana.org and accademiaitalianadellacucina.it), and the shared web-search budget ran out mid-research. All evidence comes from search-result titles, URLs and snippets seen by the researchers, plus the checkers' desk review. Every URL in this file appeared in a real search result; none was invented by the editor. QUOTES: verified_verbatim=true means a checker (or, in three cases, the editor's own WebSearch on 11 Nov 2026) matched the exact wording against a search snippet, NOT against the live page. Northern quotes were matched by the culinary checker against the researchers' search transcripts; Southern quotes by the sources checker against the researcher's search excerpts; the only Roman quote kept by a checker is the Il Nordest headline. Editor-verified via WebSearch snippets: the Amatriciana STG 'non prevede l'impiego...' sentence, Vincenzo's Plate 'NO CREAM IN CARBONARA!', and The Pasta Queen's 'Chicken alfredo really rubs me the wrong way' (found on a Nordot syndication, so a new evidence entry was added). Editor searches did NOT confirm the Dissapore carbonara garlic/onion line, the Monosilio 'consuetudine del passato' cream line, the Cracco apology wording or the Il Post chicken-pizza line, so those stay as paraphrases. All other quotes were moved into 'translation' as 'Paraphrase (exact wording not verified)', keeping the reported original wording in brackets for later checking. No pizza quote is verified. POPULARITY is a 1-5 editorial estimate of how often and how loudly Italians complain, taken as the lower of the two checker lenses; it is not a measured count. Only the YouGov 2022 net scores (ketchup on pasta -82, pineapple on pizza -63, cream in carbonara -45, cheese on seafood pasta -39, Bolognese on spaghetti +81) are survey numbers, and they come from write-ups of the survey. Very recent items (2026: Franco Pepe/AGI 5 Nov, Brisbane chef firing 8 Nov, La Voce di New York 2 Nov, the Jubany ragù, the Carbonara Day 2026 survey percentages, the La Russa Senate Norma) could not be re-checked. Sweep-only intruders and the tiramisù dish were never reviewed by a checker lens and are flagged in review_status/coverage. Influencer chefs not reached for these dishes: Benedetta Rossi, Giorgio Locatelli, Gabriele Bonci, Enzo Coccia, Davide Civitiello. Real people's names appear only in contested_note, evidence, controversies and the chef list; 'why', 'game_line', 'game_blurb' and 'game_method' use archetypes, per the project rule in docs/RESEARCH.md. contested_note and viral_controversies texts still name people and companies and must be generalised before any in-game use. To finish verification, allow those hosts in the session's network settings (or raise the search budget) and re-open each cited page before printing a quote verbatim.
disagreements_resolved: Popularity: every lens-reviewed intruder takes the LOWER score of the two lenses (e.g. carbonara garlic 4->3, peas 3->2, milk 2->1; gricia onion 4->3; Alfredo garlic 4->2 and broccoli 3->2; ragù cream 4->3; pesto cashews 4->3; vongole tomato 3->2; aglio olio Parmigiano 4->3 and butter 2->1; Norma Parmigiano 3->2; Margherita ketchup 4->3; capricciosa würstel 3->2; pizza-pool ketchup 4->3, BBQ 3->2, exotic meats 2->1).

Contested flags follow the culinary lens where the lenses split: pesto rocket = contested (pesto di rucola is its own Italian recipe); tortellini cooked ham = contested; tortellini plain tomato sauce = NOT contested (meat ragù is the accepted alternative, plain tomato is not); diavola bell peppers = NOT contested.

Cacio e pepe 'sodium citrate': the sources lens removed it (its only Dissapore URL says 'gel stabiliser'); the culinary lens kept it. Kept per the merge rule at popularity 1, with the note that it stands for restaurant stabilisers in general.

Aglio olio 'cream' and puttanesca 'canned pre-pitted olives': removed by the sources lens for thin or misattributed evidence, kept by the culinary lens. Kept at popularity 1 and flagged in review_status.
Amatriciana 'lard' (strutto): removed by both lenses (lard was a normal Roman cooking fat). Dropped.
Pizza-pool 'gummy sweets' and 'baked beans': added by the sources lens from the project dossier but never reviewed by the culinary lens. Not merged as intruders; listed under candidates_not_merged.

Ragù 'eggs' (2026 Spanish chef): the popular-posts sweep listed it (popularity 2) but the culinary lens had explicitly declined the lead (page never opened, unclear which ragù). Kept only as a flagged viral controversy, not an intruder.

Sweep-only carbonara intruders (mushrooms, cooked ham, white wine, parsley) and spaghetti al pomodoro 'chicken' were added with popularity 1-2 and review_status 'sweep only'. The culinary lens had left parsley and mushrooms out for lack of evidence; the sweeps then found sources (an unopened .doc guide and a 2020 Scatti di Gusto headline).

The influencer sweep marked carbonara onion as contested (old cookbooks, a chef's variant) and cacio e pepe Parmigiano as NOT contested; the culinary lens is canonical, so carbonara onion stays uncontested (variants noted) and cacio e pepe Parmigiano stays contested.
Gino D'Acampo's 2010 This Morning clip: the Roman lenses tie it to milk in carbonara, the influencer sweep to cooked ham. Both items are kept at popularity 1-2 with the conflict stated.

Texts: where the lenses' 'why', contested_note, fun facts or controversy texts differ, the editor kept the sources lens's removals (e.g. Barilla 'took the video down', Pipero's 'cat food', Carnacina and guanciale, the Alfredo jar's '24-month' Parmigiano, Gangetti, Barbieri's '30-minute' complaint, the Giovanni Rana seizure, Coldiretti/Ipsos percentages, Sorbillo's '7 euro' and Maurizio de Giovanni) and the culinary lens's corrections (e.g. 'chicken is normally a main course' rather than 'Italians never put chicken on pasta', the Accademia caveat on carbonara garlic, Artusi writing from Florence).

Canonical recipes follow the culinary lens, except details the sources lens showed to be unsupported: '1954 recipe used whole eggs' (carbonara), 'diaphragm' cut (ragù), 'only' beef and hen broth (tortellini, softened), the jarred Alfredo's '24-month' Parmigiano, the Neapolitan/Roman anchovy split (puttanesca, rests on blogs), and the brand name of the hazelnut spread.

Restored by the editor's own WebSearch: the Amatriciana STG exclusion quote (verified), the STG's 10-30% guanciale share (snippet), and Unione Sarda's report that Marchesi's 1989 carbonara used a quarter litre of cream for 400 g of pasta (snippet). Both lenses had removed the last two as unverified.

Vongole: the culinary lens flagged Vincenzo's Plate's 'waiter will look at you' quote as close to a paraphrase, while the sources lens confirmed it verbatim in a search excerpt; it is marked verified (excerpt-level).

Vongole Artusi fun fact: the culinary lens dropped onion and dried mushrooms as unverified; the sources lens had checked them against the search excerpt, so the sources-lens version is used with the culinary lens's Florence/1891 context.
Pomodoro YouGov detail (Hong Kong +79, Indonesia +76): dropped by the culinary lens, but checked against an excerpt by the sources lens; kept.
